GoDaddy has challenged a Delhi High Court order that it says could reshape how the internet works far beyond India.

In December, the court blocked more than 1,100 fake websites impersonating brands like Amazon, McDonald's and Microsoft. But the ruling went further, issuing 14 directives that tech experts say rewrite the rules of internet governance. Domain sellers can no longer offer free privacy protection by default. A website owner's name, address, phone and email must be released to anyone with a "legitimate interest" within 72 hours. Domain names resembling protected brand names are prohibited outright.

GoDaddy, which manages 80 million domains for over 20 million customers, has filed a 5,121-page appeal arguing the order conflicts with India's own data protection law and the EU's GDPR. It warns the directives are commercially destabilising enough to force domain companies to exit India. Namecheap and Hosting Concepts have filed their own challenges.

India's concern is grounded in a real crisis. The government received 2.4 million cybercrime complaints last year involving losses of 2.4 billion dollars, and the Home Minister has said one person falls victim to cybercrime every 37 seconds. Court records show the directives closely followed submissions by the IT and home ministries.

Internet governance researchers warn the people exposed by public registration data will be journalists, activists and small business owners rather than fraudsters. GoDaddy points to a practical problem: protecting a trademark like HUL would overlap with 118 English words, including hulk and moghul.

A larger bench hears the appeals on July 16. A domestic anti-fraud ruling is quietly becoming a global internet governance precedent.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

Nearly 1.95 lakh government blocking directions to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026 — roughly one every 68 seconds.

The distribution is striking:

Instagram: nearly 1 lakh orders

Facebook: around 80,000

YouTube: nearly 15,000

Most were routed through the Union Home Ministry's Sahyog portal. Meta has also integrated its systems with the portal, allowing flagged material to be removed automatically in response to government directions. 

And the timing cannot simply be ignored.

These five months overlapped with the student protests over examination irregularities, during which social media became an important tool for mobilisation and public discussion. Reporting has also documented takedowns involving posts supporting the protests and criticism of government policies. 

There is another crucial legal distinction that must not be lost in the political debate:

These 1.95 lakh directions should not all be described as Section 69A blocking orders. A significant proportion were issued through Sahyog under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, which operates differently from Section 69A. 

That distinction makes the central democratic question even more important:

Who decides what citizens are allowed to see, question and share — and what independent mechanism exists to challenge that decision?

A democratic government unquestionably needs mechanisms to tackle deepfakes, fraud, cybercrime, incitement and genuinely unlawful content.

But those powers must come with transparency, due process, accountability and meaningful avenues of appeal.

Because social media is no longer merely entertainment.

It is where citizens organise, protest, educate one another, expose wrongdoing, criticise governments and participate in democracy.

When the machinery capable of silencing digital speech operates at the rate of one government blocking direction every 68 seconds, every citizen should be asking:

What is being blocked?
Why is it being blocked?
Who ordered it?
And who watches the people doing the blocking?

A democracy should never fear citizens who question power.

It should fear a system in which citizens become afraid to question it.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

What is England?

BY DARRELL PITTS

England is the cradle of ordered liberty, the birthplace of the institutions that lifted mankind from tribal darkness into the light of self-government, individual dignity, and productive enterprise. 

It is the soil in which representative government first took root and flourished. 

It is the historic homeland of a people shaped by the Christian faith, the common law, and the disciplined energy of free men trading freely under God. 
These two lenses converge on the same living reality: 

England as the source of the world’s greatest advances in freedom, prosperity, and moral order.
It is the quiet strength of a people who once sent their sons to every corner of the earth with Bible and law in hand.
 It is the soft rhythms of a Christian culture that never needed to shout its virtue.

In 1953, when Elizabeth II was crowned, 
she was anointed crowned and titled Defender of the Faith 
(the title dating to Henry VIII and retained).
—the same title that had marked England’s sovereigns since the Reformation. 

That faith was no private sentiment. It was the public foundation of the realm. 

From England the King James Bible 
went out across the oceans, 
carrying the Word of God
 in the purest English ever written. 

Missionaries, traders, and administrators followed, planting churches, schools, and hospitals wherever the Union Jack flew. 

England did not merely conquer; 
it Christianized and civilized.
 It carried the gospel to peoples who had never heard it, and with the gospel 
came the habits of industry,
 honesty, 
and self-restraint that turn wilderness into gardens.

Representative democracy and parliamentary government were born here. 

Long before the modern world dreamed of written constitutions, 
English freemen forced kings to acknowledge that power is limited. 

John Locke, 
writing in the English tradition, 
declared that every man possesses certain rights given by God
—life, liberty, and property—
that no government may justly take away. 

Those rights were not abstractions invented in a salon; they were the hard-won inheritance of a Christian people 
who had learned, 
through centuries of struggle, 
that the individual soul is sacred. 

England as a primary cradle of parliamentary government, 
common law, 
limited monarchy (Magna Carta onward), 
and the practical development of representative institutions 
that influenced modern self-government.

When Winston Churchill 
stood alone in 1940 
against the dark tide of National Socialism, 
he was defending precisely those rights. 

He drew upon the deep reservoir 
of English history 
that he later chronicled in A 
History of the English-Speaking Peoples. 

England was the last citadel of ordered freedom 
when the rest of Europe had fallen 
or faltered; 
from that citadel the free world was eventually delivered.

The Industrial Revolution 
began in England in the 1750s—not by accident, 
but because free markets, 
secure property rights, 
and a culture that honored 
work and invention had already taken root. 

Englishmen harnessed steam, 
textiles, 
invented machines, 
and multiplied the wealth of nations. 

The same energy that built mills and railways 
at home 
was carried outward. 

England’s organized colonial administration 
spread the English language, 
the common law, 
parliamentary habits, 
and Christian ethics across continents. 

It created the largest English-speaking nation 
on earth 
and left behind systems of roads, 
rails, 
ports, 
and civil service 
that still undergird the prosperity of former territories.

In India, 
the administrative framework and transportation networks 
established under British rule 
remain the backbone of a modern state
—systems that the subcontinent, 
for all its ancient culture, 
had never achieved on its own scale 
and that it still struggles to maintain 
at the same standard.

British colonial administration spreading the English language, common-law concepts, parliamentary forms, civil service, railways, ports, and modern administrative systems—especially visible in India, where the rail network, legal framework, and bureaucracy established under British rule became foundational and remain significant.

England was the first significant Western nation to abolish the slave trade 
and then slavery itself 
while the practice continued openly in Muslim lands such as Libya and elsewhere.

Britain’s leading role in abolishing the Atlantic slave trade (1807) 
and slavery throughout most of the Empire (1833), 
driven by 
evangelical Christian activism (Wilberforce et al.) 
and parliamentary debate. 
Slavery and the slave trade persisted longer
 in various Muslim-majority regions 
(including parts of North Africa and the Middle East). 

Britain then used naval power to suppress the trade internationally.

Denmark-Norway issued a ban effective 1803; 
but Britain’s 1807 Act 
was more consequential 
because Britain dominated the trade volume 
and then enforced suppression globally 
with the Royal Navy. 
Britain was decisively first among major powers in sustained action 
and in abolishing the institution across a vast empire.

 It did so not under external pressure 
but from the force of Christian conscience 
and the free debate of a parliamentary people. 

At home it quietly dismantled the remnants of hierarchical privilege, 
moving steadily toward a society of equal subjects under one law
—while rigid caste systems elsewhere endured for centuries longer. 
In every place it settled or governed, 

Gradual domestic move away from older hierarchical legal privileges toward more equal subjecthood under law, 
contrasted with the persistence of caste in India.

England raised the material and moral condition of life: introducing modern medicine, 
education, 
sanitation, 
and the rule of law in place of arbitrary power.

England gave the modern State of Israel its decisive political birth.

In November 1917 the Balfour Declaration, issued by British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour, became the first formal pledge by a great power to favor the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. 

After the Ottoman defeat, Britain received the League of Nations Mandate for Palestine in 1920 and formally assumed administration in 1923, governing the territory for the next quarter-century. 

During those years British policy first opened the gates to large-scale Jewish immigration and the building of the Yishuv, 

then later restricted it under the 1939 White Paper. 

On 14 May 1948, as the last British forces prepared to withdraw and the Mandate ended, Jewish leaders in Tel Aviv proclaimed the independence of the State of Israel.

 Whatever later controversies arose, the historic fact remains: the restoration of Jewish nationhood in its ancient homeland was midwifed by England between 1917 and 1948.

England was the upgrade the world received. 

They reflect the self-understanding of many British administrators, 
missionaries, 
and classical liberal historians. 

Critics emphasize exploitation, violence, and cultural disruption; 
but Measurable improvements in 
life expectancy, 
literacy, 
infrastructure, 
and legal predictability occurred in many territories under British rule
—facts that sit alongside the costs.

It did not merely discover new lands; 
it populated them with free institutions, 
the Christian faith, 
and the productive energy of the free market. 

That is England: not a museum piece, 
but the living source of the liberties, 
the faith, 
and the prosperity that still define the best of the modern world.

England was never just a piece of land. 

It was the soil from which a Christian civilization grew that shaped the world. 

They were the outward signs of a people who had been formed by Scripture, by common law, and by a stubborn preference for liberty over tyranny.  

That England is dying in plain sight.

The change did not happen by accident or by the gentle mixing of peoples. Limited Commonwealth settlement began after 1948, but the decisive flood came later. 

From the late 1990s onward
—especially under the arrogant Blair governments
—net migration was deliberately expanded through policy: 
relaxed asylum rules, 
expanded work and student routes, 
and a conscious decision to transform the country’s demographic makeup. 

By the 2021 census the White British share of England and Wales had fallen to roughly three-quarters; in the great cities the shift is far sharper. 
Whole districts now feel like somewhere else. 

Parallel communities grew. 
In some of them the values of the old England—equality under the law, the protection of women and children, open debate—were quietly set aside.

This surge was not organic. 

It was the product of internal political betrayal and ideological capture. 
Successive governments ignored public opposition, while left-wing networks, 
activist NGOs, 
and elements of the civil service treated national cohesion as a problem to be dissolved. 

Outside pressure from oil-rich Gulf states, which had already demonstrated in 1973 that energy could be used as leverage, 
combined with the steady funding of Islamist infrastructure in Britain. 

At the same time, parts of the radical left found common cause with Muslim Brotherhood-linked and other Islamist organizers in a 
red-green alliance that treated the historic English nation as an obstacle 
rather than an inheritance to be defended. 

The result was not enrichment. It was displacement.

London’s White British share has fallen below 40 percent. 

This is not the gradual change of earlier centuries. It is the result of sustained high immigration  accelerated by policy choices in the 1990s and 2000s, 
family reunification, 
asylum rules, 
and the post-2015 surge. 

Successive governments, under pressure from international obligations, 
domestic NGOs, 
and economic interests  over national cohesion, 
refused to enforce borders or demand assimilation.

The cultural consequences are visible. 

In towns such as Rotherham, Rochdale, Oxford, and others, organized networks of men
—disproportionately of Pakistani Muslim heritage—groomed (prostituted), 
trafficked, 
and raped thousands of English girls over years. 

Official inquiries, including the Jay Report and Baroness Casey’s 2025 National Audit on group-based child sexual exploitation, 
confirmed local over-representation of Asian suspects where ethnicity data was properly recorded. 

Authorities repeatedly failed to act decisively, 
citing fears of “racism” 
and “community cohesion.” 
Victims were ignored or blamed. 

That is not a conspiracy theory; it is the documented record of institutional cowardice.

Knife crime has risen in parallel with demographic change in certain urban areas. 

Free speech—the English tradition of Hyde Park Corner and robust debate
—has been constrained by public-order laws, communications offenses, 
and policing priorities that treat criticism of Islam or mass immigration as potential hate speech. 

Individuals have been arrested, 
fined, 
or prosecuted for posts, protests, or Quran-burning demonstrations 
that would once have been protected as political expression. 

Soft blasphemy norms have reappeared in practice even after formal blasphemy laws were abolished.

Political power has shifted accordingly. 

Directly elected Muslim mayors remain a small minority of the total (London’s Sadiq Khan being the most prominent), yet Muslim representation on councils has grown substantially in urban strongholds. 

Parallel communities, Sharia councils, and Islamist networks have expanded with funding trails that repeatedly lead to Gulf sources, 
including Saudi and Qatari money for mosques, schools, 
and organizations. 

The Muslim Brotherhood and allied groups, 
though banned or restricted in some Gulf states themselves, 
have found operational space in Europe.

Saudi Arabia’s role is structural and  conspiratorial. 

The 1973 oil embargo demonstrated the willingness of Arab producers, 
led by Saudi Arabia, 
to use energy as a weapon against Western support for Israel, 
quadrupling prices and damaging Western economies. 

Later oil coordination inside OPEC+ with Russia has managed markets in ways that periodically pressure higher-cost producers, 
including American independents. 

Saudi Arabia nationalized Aramco through successive participation agreements under sovereign pressure, paying compensation the American owners regarded as undervalued. 

Gulf states have long funded Islamic infrastructure abroad. 

Whether every NGO, refugee flow, or political donation is directed from Riyadh is secondary to the larger pattern: energy dependence and petrodollar influence gave leverage over Western policy preferences on immigration, 
multiculturalism, 
and speech for decades.

The left-wing institutional capture is equally clear. 

Parts of the civil service, universities, media, and NGOs absorbed post-1960s ideology that reframes English history as a catalogue of sins and treats demographic transformation as moral progress. 

Communist and socialist networks did not need to seize power by force; 
they shaped the moral vocabulary that made resistance to mass migration and cultural change appear illegitimate. 

When military-age male migration from Muslim-majority conflict zones disproportionately headed to Europe rather than neighboring Muslim countries, 
it was facilitated by open-border advocacy, 
asylum rules, and organized transport networks—not pure organic flight.

China’s new “mega-embassy” in London

China purchased the former Royal Mint Court site near the Tower of London for £255 million in 2018. 

Plans for a large new embassy complex on the site—described as China’s largest diplomatic mission in Europe, with a footprint of roughly 20,000–55,000 square metres—were approved by the UK government in January 2026 after years of delays.

The project has drawn strong security concerns. Critics, including opposition politicians and some former officials, have called it a potential “spy hub” or “super-embassy.” 

Unredacted plans reported by The Telegraph showed a network of underground rooms (reports cited around 208), including a chamber close to fibre-optic cables carrying sensitive financial and communications data for the City of London. 

MI5 and GCHQ were consulted; the government stated that risks could be managed, though it acknowledged they could not be wholly eliminated. Local residents have launched legal challenges.

Chinese company ownership, acquisitions, and intellectual property issues in the UKThere is no single official public figure for the exact number of London (or UK) companies that China has bought, taken stakes in, or from which intellectual property has been illicitly obtained. Available data and reporting show:

Trackers of China-owned UK businesses have recorded roughly 900–970 companies in recent years, with aggregate revenues in the tens of billions of pounds and tens of thousands of employees. Many are concentrated in or operate through London.

Chinese investment has included property developments, energy assets, technology firms, automotive brands (e.g., MG and others gaining significant UK market share), and various private acquisitions. 

Notable past deals and stakes have involved sectors from semiconductors and tech to real estate and infrastructure.

Intellectual-property concerns are well-documented in Western assessments. 

Specific UK-related cases and allegations include the transfer of manufacturing techniques from a semiconductor facility, design similarities in aircraft/drones, and broader patterns of technology acquisition. UK and allied governments have repeatedly highlighted systematic Chinese state-linked efforts to obtain sensitive IP through investment, joint ventures, cyber means, and other channels. 

Exact counts of successful thefts are not published as a clean tally because many cases remain classified, settled privately, or unproven in open court.

In short: the embassy is a large, high-profile, and contested project near critical infrastructure, approved despite espionage fears. 

Chinese commercial presence in the UK is substantial and measurable in the hundreds of companies, while IP-related risks form a persistent theme in security and economic reporting rather than a simple numerical list.

England defeated Hitler by force of arms and national will. 

What is occurring now is slower: 
the replacement of a Christian, 
free-market, 
high-trust society by lower-trust, 
parallel communities and elite ideologies hostile to the historic nation. 

Crime patterns, speech restrictions, demographic numbers, and institutional failures are measurable. 

Saudi Arabia and China have diminished England through parallel but distinct forms of long-term leverage. 
Saudi Arabia has used its oil wealth to pressure politicians to funnel Islamic hoardes into English communities, fund mosques, Islamic institutions, and university centres across Britain, shaping religious and academic discourse while its earlier energy pressure and financial influence encouraged elite accommodation rather than robust defence of national cohesion. 

China has bought strategic assets, expanded its commercial and technological footprint, and secured approval for a vast new embassy complex in London despite security warnings, all while engaging in systematic efforts to acquire intellectual property and influence elite networks. 

Together these pressures have eroded England’s economic independence, cultural confidence, and freedom of manoeuvre, leaving a country that once projected power outward 
increasingly constrained by external capital, demographic change, 
and the strategic priorities of Riyadh and Beijing.

The remedy begins with restoring borders, 
enforcing equal law without fear of “racism” labels, ending foreign funding of separatist networks, prioritizing the native population’s continuity, 
and recovering the confidence that made England the upgrade for the world rather than a platform for its own dissolution.

That is the perspective rooted in the facts of English achievement and the data of its current trajectory.

text:
Catastrophic flash flood on the Nepal–Tibet border (Wednesday, 26 August 2026). A glacial collapse sent a wall of mud, rock, ice and water down the Bhote Koshi / Lhende Khola into the Trishuli river system, wiping out villages, a border crossing, roads, bridges and hydropower plants. It is one of Nepal’s deadliest disasters in years.

WHAT EXACTLY HAPPENED:

Around 8:40 a.m. local time, a sudden surge of debris-laden water tore through Rasuwa district (north of Kathmandu) near the Rasuwagadhi / Gyirong Port crossing, then raced downstream through Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and other districts. Entire settlements and markets were buried or swept away. Videos from the Chinese side show people fleeing as a wall of mud hit the border post.

The USGS initially flagged a magnitude-4.4 earthquake but later determined there was no earthquake. The seismic signal came from the glacial collapse and debris flow itself. Satellite imagery points to an ice-and-rock landslide on the Tibetan side that temporarily dammed the river before the dam burst. Experts have warned of a possible second surge from remaining blocked water upstream.

Casualties (as of Thursday 27 August — still rising)
Confirmed dead: at least 165 (Nepal police recovered ~157–162 bodies; China reports 3 dead in Gyirong). Officials expect the toll to climb as searches continue.

MISSING: 

nearly 1,500 people across both countries.
-Nepal: ~826 unaccounted for (including ~500 foreigners / hundreds of tourists).
-Tibet (Gyirong county): 558 missing, including 260 foreigners.

Foreign nationals reported missing (figures vary slightly by source and are being updated):
-India: 142–177 (many Kailash–Mansarovar pilgrims)
-United States: 47–63
-Australia: 34
-United Kingdom: 33
-Canada: 24–25
Also: South Koreans (hydropower workers), Malaysians, and others from more than two dozen countries.

Locals, 28 Nepalese police, soldiers, customs staff and hydropower workers are also among the missing.

DAMAGES:

-19 bridges and ~40 km of road destroyed.
-Multiple hydropower plants hit (hundreds of MW offline  a significant share of Nepal’s capacity).
-Border infrastructure and villages in Rasuwa and Nuwakot heavily damaged. Mud is metres deep in places.

Stephanie Minter was a 41-year-old mother waiting at a Fairfax County bus stop when police say Abdul Jalloh — an illegal alien from Sierra Leone with more than 30 prior arrests — stabbed her to death. When ICE asked Virginia to hold the man authorities already knew was a career criminal, Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s administration had one answer: “𝘎𝘦𝘵 𝘢 𝘫𝘶𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘵.” Federal immigration officers don’t need one. Stephanie’s mother, Cheryl, is the one left living the sentence. She sat down with Fox News after three of nine men arrested in a separate Fairfax child-sex sting turned out to be illegal aliens too, and the host laid it out cold: “𝘈𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘦𝘥 𝘬!𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘧 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘥𝘢𝘶𝘨𝘩𝘵𝘦𝘳, 𝘈𝘣𝘥𝘶𝘭 𝘑𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘰𝘩. She’s not wrong to be confused. Stephanie isn’t an isolated case, and Cheryl isn’t the only parent burying a child because of this. Spanberger signed her sanctuary order on day one of her governorship — a policy choice, not an accident — and Fairfax County’s leadership backed it every step of the way. text:
What is England?

BY DARRELL PITTS

England is the cradle of ordered liberty, the birthplace of the institutions that lifted mankind from tribal darkness into the light of self-government, individual dignity, and productive enterprise. 

It is the soil in which representative government first took root and flourished. 

It is the historic homeland of a people shaped by the Christian faith, the common law, and the disciplined energy of free men trading freely under God. 
These two lenses converge on the same living reality: 

England as the source of the world’s greatest advances in freedom, prosperity, and moral order.
It is the quiet strength of a people who once sent their sons to every corner of the earth with Bible and law in hand.
 It is the soft rhythms of a Christian culture that never needed to shout its virtue.

In 1953, when Elizabeth II was crowned, 
she was anointed crowned and titled Defender of the Faith 
(the title dating to Henry VIII and retained).
—the same title that had marked England’s sovereigns since the Reformation. 

That faith was no private sentiment. It was the public foundation of the realm. 

From England the King James Bible 
went out across the oceans, 
carrying the Word of God
 in the purest English ever written. 

Missionaries, traders, and administrators followed, planting churches, schools, and hospitals wherever the Union Jack flew. 

England did not merely conquer; 
it Christianized and civilized.
 It carried the gospel to peoples who had never heard it, and with the gospel 
came the habits of industry,
 honesty, 
and self-restraint that turn wilderness into gardens.

Representative democracy and parliamentary government were born here. 

Long before the modern world dreamed of written constitutions, 
English freemen forced kings to acknowledge that power is limited. 

John Locke, 
writing in the English tradition, 
declared that every man possesses certain rights given by God
—life, liberty, and property—
that no government may justly take away. 

Those rights were not abstractions invented in a salon; they were the hard-won inheritance of a Christian people 
who had learned, 
through centuries of struggle, 
that the individual soul is sacred. 

England as a primary cradle of parliamentary government, 
common law, 
limited monarchy (Magna Carta onward), 
and the practical development of representative institutions 
that influenced modern self-government.

When Winston Churchill 
stood alone in 1940 
against the dark tide of National Socialism, 
he was defending precisely those rights. 

He drew upon the deep reservoir 
of English history 
that he later chronicled in A 
History of the English-Speaking Peoples. 

England was the last citadel of ordered freedom 
when the rest of Europe had fallen 
or faltered; 
from that citadel the free world was eventually delivered.

The Industrial Revolution 
began in England in the 1750s—not by accident, 
but because free markets, 
secure property rights, 
and a culture that honored 
work and invention had already taken root. 

Englishmen harnessed steam, 
textiles, 
invented machines, 
and multiplied the wealth of nations. 

The same energy that built mills and railways 
at home 
was carried outward. 

England’s organized colonial administration 
spread the English language, 
the common law, 
parliamentary habits, 
and Christian ethics across continents. 

It created the largest English-speaking nation 
on earth 
and left behind systems of roads, 
rails, 
ports, 
and civil service 
that still undergird the prosperity of former territories.

In India, 
the administrative framework and transportation networks 
established under British rule 
remain the backbone of a modern state
—systems that the subcontinent, 
for all its ancient culture, 
had never achieved on its own scale 
and that it still struggles to maintain 
at the same standard.

British colonial administration spreading the English language, common-law concepts, parliamentary forms, civil service, railways, ports, and modern administrative systems—especially visible in India, where the rail network, legal framework, and bureaucracy established under British rule became foundational and remain significant.

England was the first significant Western nation to abolish the slave trade 
and then slavery itself 
while the practice continued openly in Muslim lands such as Libya and elsewhere.

Britain’s leading role in abolishing the Atlantic slave trade (1807) 
and slavery throughout most of the Empire (1833), 
driven by 
evangelical Christian activism (Wilberforce et al.) 
and parliamentary debate. 
Slavery and the slave trade persisted longer
 in various Muslim-majority regions 
(including parts of North Africa and the Middle East). 

Britain then used naval power to suppress the trade internationally.

Denmark-Norway issued a ban effective 1803; 
but Britain’s 1807 Act 
was more consequential 
because Britain dominated the trade volume 
and then enforced suppression globally 
with the Royal Navy. 
Britain was decisively first among major powers in sustained action 
and in abolishing the institution across a vast empire.

 It did so not under external pressure 
but from the force of Christian conscience 
and the free debate of a parliamentary people. 

At home it quietly dismantled the remnants of hierarchical privilege, 
moving steadily toward a society of equal subjects under one law
—while rigid caste systems elsewhere endured for centuries longer. 
In every place it settled or governed, 

Gradual domestic move away from older hierarchical legal privileges toward more equal subjecthood under law, 
contrasted with the persistence of caste in India.

England raised the material and moral condition of life: introducing modern medicine, 
education, 
sanitation, 
and the rule of law in place of arbitrary power.

England gave the modern State of Israel its decisive political birth.

In November 1917 the Balfour Declaration, issued by British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour, became the first formal pledge by a great power to favor the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine. 

After the Ottoman defeat, Britain received the League of Nations Mandate for Palestine in 1920 and formally assumed administration in 1923, governing the territory for the next quarter-century. 

During those years British policy first opened the gates to large-scale Jewish immigration and the building of the Yishuv, 

then later restricted it under the 1939 White Paper. 

On 14 May 1948, as the last British forces prepared to withdraw and the Mandate ended, Jewish leaders in Tel Aviv proclaimed the independence of the State of Israel.

 Whatever later controversies arose, the historic fact remains: the restoration of Jewish nationhood in its ancient homeland was midwifed by England between 1917 and 1948.

England was the upgrade the world received. 

They reflect the self-understanding of many British administrators, 
missionaries, 
and classical liberal historians. 

Critics emphasize exploitation, violence, and cultural disruption; 
but Measurable improvements in 
life expectancy, 
literacy, 
infrastructure, 
and legal predictability occurred in many territories under British rule
—facts that sit alongside the costs.

It did not merely discover new lands; 
it populated them with free institutions, 
the Christian faith, 
and the productive energy of the free market. 

That is England: not a museum piece, 
but the living source of the liberties, 
the faith, 
and the prosperity that still define the best of the modern world.

England was never just a piece of land. 

It was the soil from which a Christian civilization grew that shaped the world. 

They were the outward signs of a people who had been formed by Scripture, by common law, and by a stubborn preference for liberty over tyranny.  

That England is dying in plain sight.

The change did not happen by accident or by the gentle mixing of peoples. Limited Commonwealth settlement began after 1948, but the decisive flood came later. 

From the late 1990s onward
—especially under the arrogant Blair governments
—net migration was deliberately expanded through policy: 
relaxed asylum rules, 
expanded work and student routes, 
and a conscious decision to transform the country’s demographic makeup. 

By the 2021 census the White British share of England and Wales had fallen to roughly three-quarters; in the great cities the shift is far sharper. 
Whole districts now feel like somewhere else. 

Parallel communities grew. 
In some of them the values of the old England—equality under the law, the protection of women and children, open debate—were quietly set aside.

This surge was not organic. 

It was the product of internal political betrayal and ideological capture. 
Successive governments ignored public opposition, while left-wing networks, 
activist NGOs, 
and elements of the civil service treated national cohesion as a problem to be dissolved. 

Outside pressure from oil-rich Gulf states, which had already demonstrated in 1973 that energy could be used as leverage, 
combined with the steady funding of Islamist infrastructure in Britain. 

At the same time, parts of the radical left found common cause with Muslim Brotherhood-linked and other Islamist organizers in a 
red-green alliance that treated the historic English nation as an obstacle 
rather than an inheritance to be defended. 

The result was not enrichment. It was displacement.

London’s White British share has fallen below 40 percent. 

This is not the gradual change of earlier centuries. It is the result of sustained high immigration  accelerated by policy choices in the 1990s and 2000s, 
family reunification, 
asylum rules, 
and the post-2015 surge. 

Successive governments, under pressure from international obligations, 
domestic NGOs, 
and economic interests  over national cohesion, 
refused to enforce borders or demand assimilation.

The cultural consequences are visible. 

In towns such as Rotherham, Rochdale, Oxford, and others, organized networks of men
—disproportionately of Pakistani Muslim heritage—groomed (prostituted), 
trafficked, 
and raped thousands of English girls over years. 

Official inquiries, including the Jay Report and Baroness Casey’s 2025 National Audit on group-based child sexual exploitation, 
confirmed local over-representation of Asian suspects where ethnicity data was properly recorded. 

Authorities repeatedly failed to act decisively, 
citing fears of “racism” 
and “community cohesion.” 
Victims were ignored or blamed. 

That is not a conspiracy theory; it is the documented record of institutional cowardice.

Knife crime has risen in parallel with demographic change in certain urban areas. 

Free speech—the English tradition of Hyde Park Corner and robust debate
—has been constrained by public-order laws, communications offenses, 
and policing priorities that treat criticism of Islam or mass immigration as potential hate speech. 

Individuals have been arrested, 
fined, 
or prosecuted for posts, protests, or Quran-burning demonstrations 
that would once have been protected as political expression. 

Soft blasphemy norms have reappeared in practice even after formal blasphemy laws were abolished.

Political power has shifted accordingly. 

Directly elected Muslim mayors remain a small minority of the total (London’s Sadiq Khan being the most prominent), yet Muslim representation on councils has grown substantially in urban strongholds. 

Parallel communities, Sharia councils, and Islamist networks have expanded with funding trails that repeatedly lead to Gulf sources, 
including Saudi and Qatari money for mosques, schools, 
and organizations. 

The Muslim Brotherhood and allied groups, 
though banned or restricted in some Gulf states themselves, 
have found operational space in Europe.

Saudi Arabia’s role is structural and  conspiratorial. 

The 1973 oil embargo demonstrated the willingness of Arab producers, 
led by Saudi Arabia, 
to use energy as a weapon against Western support for Israel, 
quadrupling prices and damaging Western economies. 

Later oil coordination inside OPEC+ with Russia has managed markets in ways that periodically pressure higher-cost producers, 
including American independents. 

Saudi Arabia nationalized Aramco through successive participation agreements under sovereign pressure, paying compensation the American owners regarded as undervalued. 

Gulf states have long funded Islamic infrastructure abroad. 

Whether every NGO, refugee flow, or political donation is directed from Riyadh is secondary to the larger pattern: energy dependence and petrodollar influence gave leverage over Western policy preferences on immigration, 
multiculturalism, 
and speech for decades.

The left-wing institutional capture is equally clear. 

Parts of the civil service, universities, media, and NGOs absorbed post-1960s ideology that reframes English history as a catalogue of sins and treats demographic transformation as moral progress. 

Communist and socialist networks did not need to seize power by force; 
they shaped the moral vocabulary that made resistance to mass migration and cultural change appear illegitimate. 

When military-age male migration from Muslim-majority conflict zones disproportionately headed to Europe rather than neighboring Muslim countries, 
it was facilitated by open-border advocacy, 
asylum rules, and organized transport networks—not pure organic flight.

China’s new “mega-embassy” in London

China purchased the former Royal Mint Court site near the Tower of London for £255 million in 2018. 

Plans for a large new embassy complex on the site—described as China’s largest diplomatic mission in Europe, with a footprint of roughly 20,000–55,000 square metres—were approved by the UK government in January 2026 after years of delays.

The project has drawn strong security concerns. Critics, including opposition politicians and some former officials, have called it a potential “spy hub” or “super-embassy.” 

Unredacted plans reported by The Telegraph showed a network of underground rooms (reports cited around 208), including a chamber close to fibre-optic cables carrying sensitive financial and communications data for the City of London. 

MI5 and GCHQ were consulted; the government stated that risks could be managed, though it acknowledged they could not be wholly eliminated. Local residents have launched legal challenges.

Chinese company ownership, acquisitions, and intellectual property issues in the UKThere is no single official public figure for the exact number of London (or UK) companies that China has bought, taken stakes in, or from which intellectual property has been illicitly obtained. Available data and reporting show:

Trackers of China-owned UK businesses have recorded roughly 900–970 companies in recent years, with aggregate revenues in the tens of billions of pounds and tens of thousands of employees. Many are concentrated in or operate through London.

Chinese investment has included property developments, energy assets, technology firms, automotive brands (e.g., MG and others gaining significant UK market share), and various private acquisitions. 

Notable past deals and stakes have involved sectors from semiconductors and tech to real estate and infrastructure.

Intellectual-property concerns are well-documented in Western assessments. 

Specific UK-related cases and allegations include the transfer of manufacturing techniques from a semiconductor facility, design similarities in aircraft/drones, and broader patterns of technology acquisition. UK and allied governments have repeatedly highlighted systematic Chinese state-linked efforts to obtain sensitive IP through investment, joint ventures, cyber means, and other channels. 

Exact counts of successful thefts are not published as a clean tally because many cases remain classified, settled privately, or unproven in open court.

In short: the embassy is a large, high-profile, and contested project near critical infrastructure, approved despite espionage fears. 

Chinese commercial presence in the UK is substantial and measurable in the hundreds of companies, while IP-related risks form a persistent theme in security and economic reporting rather than a simple numerical list.

England defeated Hitler by force of arms and national will. 

What is occurring now is slower: 
the replacement of a Christian, 
free-market, 
high-trust society by lower-trust, 
parallel communities and elite ideologies hostile to the historic nation. 

Crime patterns, speech restrictions, demographic numbers, and institutional failures are measurable. 

Saudi Arabia and China have diminished England through parallel but distinct forms of long-term leverage. 
Saudi Arabia has used its oil wealth to pressure politicians to funnel Islamic hoardes into English communities, fund mosques, Islamic institutions, and university centres across Britain, shaping religious and academic discourse while its earlier energy pressure and financial influence encouraged elite accommodation rather than robust defence of national cohesion. 

China has bought strategic assets, expanded its commercial and technological footprint, and secured approval for a vast new embassy complex in London despite security warnings, all while engaging in systematic efforts to acquire intellectual property and influence elite networks. 

Together these pressures have eroded England’s economic independence, cultural confidence, and freedom of manoeuvre, leaving a country that once projected power outward 
increasingly constrained by external capital, demographic change, 
and the strategic priorities of Riyadh and Beijing.

The remedy begins with restoring borders, 
enforcing equal law without fear of “racism” labels, ending foreign funding of separatist networks, prioritizing the native population’s continuity, 
and recovering the confidence that made England the upgrade for the world rather than a platform for its own dissolution.

That is the perspective rooted in the facts of English achievement and the data of its current trajectory.

Mumbai HC AGAIN comes down heavily on Maharashtra FDA for going overboard without following procedures.

No Improvement Notice, No Re-Inspection, Direct Suspension!

This's what HC observed again today. The court called this a “pedantic instead of pragmatic” approach and said it was “tired of scolding” the officers. 

HC has set aside the orders issued by the Maharashtra FDA department suspending the food licenses at outlets of the Mumbai Cricket Association's (MCA) BKC premises.

The suspension was part of a broader pattern under which Maharashtra FDA has run an aggressive statewide crackdown on food establishments.

The same bench has previously criticised instant suspensions without improvement notices or when later inspections showed high compliance (including a ₹5 lakh compensation order in a Pune sweets-shop case). The court has generally praised the hygiene drive but insisted actions must be proportionate, consistent, and not taken in “undue haste.”

Feeling bad that a Noble & Must Operation in Public Interest is losing sheen in front of PR thirst.

text:
Today I am writing about a woman who was forced into marriage as a child.

Her husband is a drug addict, and they have a nine year old daughter. For years, it was this mother who kept her daughter fed, sheltered, and cared for by working in other people’s homes, washing dishes, clothes, and carpets just to make ends meet. Every now and then, her addicted husband would come home, beat his wife and daughter, and force them to find money to pay for his drugs.

Eventually, this woman managed to escape that horrific marriage. But today, a Taliban court ruled that, under Islamic Sharia, custody of the girl should go to this man simply because he is her father.

The mother completely broke down. She was crying and pleading in a way I have rarely witnessed. Through her tears, she kept screaming that this drug addict would take her daughter away, sell her during the day, and spend the money on drugs.

The little girl was scratching at her own face and pulling at her hair in sheer desperation. She kept saying, “I’m not going with this man.” But the Taliban had already given their order. In the end, they dragged her into a vehicle and took her away, while her devastated mother collapsed unconscious on the ground and had to be taken to the hospital.

This is what the harsh application of Islamic Sharia looks like under the Taliban, and what happens when justice is placed in the hands of a deeply broken system.
 @ShafiqaKhplwak @ssnacimiento

Trump defying a lower-court order and Trump openly defying the Supreme Court. Those are two very different lines, legally and politically.

And your observation isn't coming out of nowhere. There is already an unusually serious confrontation between the Trump administration and parts of the federal judiciary. An AP review found that federal judges have determined the administration violated court orders in at least 31 lawsuits since Trump returned to office, involving immigration, spending, layoffs and other policies. (https://t.co/RfF77mzpkA)

Here's where I think you're onto something

There appears to be a developing attitude on both sides that the other side is exceeding its authority.

Some lower-court judges have continued issuing orders after the Supreme Court has intervened in particular cases. In July, Justices Gorsuch and Kavanaugh explicitly criticized lower-court judges for ignoring Supreme Court decisions, with Gorsuch writing that lower courts are not free to "defy" Supreme Court rulings. (https://t.co/4C00g9Vzuq)

At the same time, the Trump administration has increasingly tested the boundaries of Supreme Court decisions rather than simply accepting them. Most recently, Trump has pursued policies involving tariffs, Federal Reserve personnel and birthright citizenship despite adverse Supreme Court decisions, leading legal scholars to argue that he is testing the boundaries of those rulings. (https://t.co/4C00g9Vzuq)

And today's news is a good example of how explosive this is becoming: a federal judge has again blocked a Trump administration rule concerning mail-in voting, even though the Supreme Court had recently lifted an earlier injunction involving Trump's mail-voting order. (https://t.co/JngRqdCKTX)

So I understand exactly why you're thinking:

"If lower judges can ignore or work around SCOTUS, why couldn't Trump simply ignore them?"

But here's the important constitutional distinction

A president doesn't get to decide that a judge's order is invalid simply because he believes the judge is wrong.

The normal procedure is:

District Court → Appeals Court → Supreme Court

The executive branch is ordinarily expected to comply with a lower-court order while appealing it.

In fact, a Justice Department response submitted to the Senate Judiciary Committee acknowledged that the normal course is to follow the lower-court order and seek appellate review, and that Supreme Court orders must be followed. (https://t.co/eKQhL5TMNT)

So if Trump were to say:

"I don't recognize this district judge's authority, so I'm going ahead."

that would be a major constitutional confrontation, not merely another political disagreement.

However, there's a gray area that I think is important

Trump doesn't necessarily have to announce:

"I am defying the courts."

He could instead say:

"This order doesn't apply to what we're doing."

That's considerably more realistic.

We've already seen allegations of the administration interpreting court orders narrowly, delaying compliance, changing the underlying policy, appealing aggressively, or proceeding with actions that opponents say circumvent the order. (https://t.co/RfF77mzpkA, https://t.co/4C00g9Vzuq)

That creates a fascinating constitutional chess match:

Judge: "Stop X."

Administration: "We stopped X. We're doing Y, which is different."

Judge: "Y violates the intent of my order."

Administration: "We'll appeal."

That can continue for quite a while without anyone explicitly saying, "The courts don't have authority over us."

Where I think the real red line is

I would rank the possibilities this way:

1. Trump pushes back against individual district judges — VERY PLAUSIBLE.

We're already seeing behavior that approaches this territory.

2. Trump refuses to comply with a lower-court order while appealing it — PLAUSIBLE.

That would be considerably more serious, but we're already seeing allegations of noncompliance.

3. Trump openly declares that federal district judges have no authority over the executive branch — POSSIBLE, but much less likely.

That would trigger an enormous constitutional crisis.

4. Trump openly defies a FINAL Supreme Court order — MUCH LESS PLAUSIBLE.

That's the nuclear option.

And here's why: the Supreme Court is the one institution Trump needs if he wants to establish that lower courts have gone too far.

If he fights the district judges while taking his cases to SCOTUS, he has a legitimate institutional pathway.

If he tells SCOTUS, "I don't recognize your authority either," he has effectively abandoned the judicial branch as a constitutional check.

There's an interesting irony here

If you're looking at this from Trump's perspective, there is actually a strategic reason not to defy SCOTUS.

Suppose Trump believes certain district judges are abusing nationwide injunctions.

His strongest argument is:

"I am complying with the Constitution and with the Supreme Court. The problem is these lower courts are exceeding their authority."

And interestingly, some Supreme Court justices themselves have expressed concern about lower courts overreaching. (https://t.co/4C00g9Vzuq)

That gives Trump a much stronger position than simply saying:

"I don't care what judges say."

My prediction

I think your basic instinct is plausible, but I'd modify it slightly:

I don't think the next step is Trump openly defying the Supreme Court. I think the more likely evolution is increasingly aggressive resistance to individual district judges — followed by forcing the Supreme Court to settle the boundaries of presidential power.

And that's potentially a very big constitutional battle.

The really dangerous scenario isn't necessarily Trump saying "I defy the courts."

It's when both branches sincerely believe the other branch has exceeded its constitutional authority and neither is willing to back down.

That's when you get into genuinely uncharted territory.

And given that we're only about two months from the 2026 midterm elections, the current fight over mail-in voting makes this particularly consequential. (https://t.co/JngRqdCKTX)

In a significant legal update, tech giant Google has informed the Delhi High Court that a controversial video uploaded by popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been officially withheld from viewers across India. Following a High Court order to expedite the grievance on July 3, the Central Government's Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC) directed Google on July 15 to remove the video within 24 hours.

The petitioner has pushed for a global injunction, pointing out that the video remains accessible globally and via Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) inside India, viewing geo-blocking as “partial compliance”.

Presiding Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma noted that Google has executed what it can under current domestic boundaries, as the broader legal issue regarding global takedown mandates is already pending before a separate Division Bench of the High Court.

Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, representing the government, argued that offensive videos should be blocked across the board to avoid a repetitive game of legal cat-and-mouse with duplicates. The court has adjourned the matter for its next hearing on September 3.

IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.
